title: The Seizure on the Intercom (Darley & Latane, 1968)

youtube.title: Someone Is Having a Seizure. Would You Get Up? #Shorts
youtube.description:
You're alone in a small room. Through the intercom, another student starts choking and begging for help.
Do you get up, or do you wait for someone else?

This is Darley and Latane's 1968 bystander experiment, told from the inside. Alone, about 85% of people went for help before the seizure ended. When they thought four others could hear it too, only about 31% did.

If you're one of many, would YOU be the one who moves? Tell me in the comments.

Sources:
- Darley, J. M., & Latane, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377-383.
- The New York Times, editor's note on the 1964 Kitty Genovese coverage (2016).

#psychology #bystandereffect #socialpsychology #shorts #mindset

sources: Darley, J. M., & Latane, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. JPSP 8(4), 377-383: students talked over an intercom, one mic on at a time; the 'victim' was a tape recording.
Same study: alone with the victim, about 85% reported the seizure before it ended; believing four others also heard it, about 31%.
1964 New York Times report of 38 witnesses to the Kitty Genovese murder; the Times' 2016 editor's note said the story grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they perceived.
lines: You're sitting alone in a small room. Through an intercom, you hear another student start to choke, and beg for help.
Nineteen sixty-eight, New York. You signed up to talk about college life. Everyone talks through headphones, so nobody can see anyone.
Earlier, one student said he sometimes gets seizures. Now his voice breaks. He says he's going to die.
But you think other students are listening too. Surely someone else has already gone. So you sit there, and wait.
When people thought they were the only listener, about eighty-five percent ran for help before the seizure ended.
When they thought four others could hear it, only about thirty-one percent did. More people, less help.
There was no seizure. The voice was a tape. The only thing being tested was whether you would stand up.
The study was inspired by a murder where a newspaper said thirty-eight people did nothing. That story was exaggerated. This result was not.
In a crowd, everyone waits for someone else. So next time, will you be the one who moves?
